Learning Objectives
Describe the indications for the nonsurgical management of hip osteoarthritis.
Discuss treatment options for the management of hip osteoarthritis according to the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline on the
Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hip and the literature supporting each treatment option.
Review the contraindications to the nonsurgical management of hip osteoarthritis.
Recognize the limitations and risks of nonsurgical management of hip osteoarthritis.
Diagnosis
Not all groin pain is hip arthritis; a physical examination and patient history can differentiate
orthopaedic and non-orthopaedic causes of groin pain.

Imaging studies, starting with plain radiographs, may help determine musculoskeletal
pathology causing hip pain. 
Weight bearing AP pelvis radiographs are a good imaging study for the detection of arthritis. 

Diagnosis
Osteoarthritis is a common cause of adult hip pain. Correct diagnosis before nonsurgical
management is paramount because some pathologies are not appropriately managed
nonsurgically and necessitate surgical management. Patients may present with myriad
underlying causes for their pain, including tumors, infections, fractures, inflammatory
arthropathies, osteonecrosis, transient osteoporosis of the hip, abductor tears,
trochanteric bursitis, labral tears, and impingement syndromes.
A careful patient history and physical examination aid in triaging possible etiologies of
hip pain and will identify patients who may benefit from degenerative hip pain
treatment. Appropriate nonsurgical treatment strategies for adult patients with
osteoarthritis are paramount. After a diagnosis of hip osteoarthritis is made, usually via
radiographs, and the patient’s pain is found to be caused by arthritis, some nonsurgical
treatment options may be considered. Short of hip replacement, no known cure exists
for hip arthritis, and no approved method for regeneration of hip articular cartilage is
available (Resource 1).
The nonsurgical management of hip osteoarthritis involves symptom management. This
can be achieved via anti-inflammatory medications (oral NSAIDs and corticosteroid
injections), by decreasing hip joint reactive forces with the use of walking aids or weight
loss, and via pain modulation with physical therapy.
Patient Selection

Total hip arthroplasty (THA) is one of the most valuable surgical treatment options. THA is
associated with a good safety profile for most patients and results in a considerable
improvement in quality of life of patients with severe arthritis.
Nonsurgical management of hip arthritis is most useful in patients with mild disease and
patients with severe comorbidities.

Patient Selection
Total hip arthroplasty (THA) was introduced and popularized during the 1960s and
1970s. Advances in implant technology and surgical technique have increased the
personal and societal benefits of THA. The benefits of the nonsurgical management of
hip osteoarthritis must be measured against the benefits of THA. Because THA is such a
successful surgical procedure, the threshold for THA is lower than that for total knee
arthroplasty. The clinical improvement-to-risk ratio associated with THA is better than
that of almost all other surgical procedures.
Clinical assessment tools may aid in the surgical decision-making process between THA
and nonsurgical management of hip arthritis. These tools include the EQ-5D, the Medical
Outcomes Study 36-Item Short Form, the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities
Osteoarthritis Index, the American Society of Anesthesiologists classification system, the
Charlson Comorbidity Index, and the Elixhauser Comorbidity Index. These tools may be
reasonable estimators of perioperative complications after THA. This type of data can be
used to inform patients of their relative risk associated with surgical treatment and,
therefore, help them decide whether to proceed with surgical treatment or continue
nonsurgical treatment. Although these risk assessment tools can be used to set
expectations regarding perioperative adverse events, they do not provide an estimate of
the value of surgical treatment for each patient. A patient with debilitating hip pain and
numerous comorbidities may wish to risk the high probability of a serious adverse event
for the improvement in function associated with THA. Value assessment calculators for
this type of decision making are lacking.

Therefore, the decision to proceed with nonsurgical treatment versus THA for the
management of hip arthritis involves shared decision making between the patient and
the surgeon. The standard of care after a new diagnosis of hip arthritis generally is
nonsurgical treatment followed by THA only after the patient has exhausted reasonable
nonsurgical treatment modalities. This strategy follows cultural, legal, and financial
constraints on the medical system but is not necessarily evidence based. No clear
evidence shows that patients benefit from a trial of nonsurgical treatment before
undergoing THA; however, that is the accepted standard in orthopaedic care.
In 2017, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) published an Evidence-
Based Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hip.1 This
guideline summarizes several nonsurgical treatment options for the management of hip
osteoarthritis based on available literature and grades the recommendations based on
the strength of the supporting evidence. Three recommendations received the strongest
support for use: non-narcotic management (use of NSAIDs to manage arthritic pain),
intra-articular corticosteroids, and physical therapy as a nonsurgical treatment option. In
addition, the guideline cites strong evidence against the use of intra-articular hyaluronic
acid for the management of hip osteoarthritis (Resource 2).
Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs
Several randomized controlled trials have shown the efficacy of NSAIDs in improving pain and
function related to hip osteoarthritis.2-4
NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, lowering the formation of inflammatory- and
pain-generating prostaglandins.
NSAIDs are categorized as nonselective or selective. Nonselective NSAIDs bind to COX-1 and
COX-2 enzymes, whereas selective NSAIDs bind preferentially to COX-2. The most common
adverse effect of NSAIDs, gastrointestinal effects, are thought to be related to the inhibition of
COX-1. Selective NSAIDs are associated with fewer gastrointestinal adverse effects. NSAIDs
have a spectrum of activity between COX-1 and COX-2 inhibition.
Contraindications and Adverse Effects

4/12

The most common adverse effect of NSAID use is dyspepsia. The inhibition of prostaglandin
production through COX inhibition results in decreased mucus production in the
gastrointestinal lining. Long-term use may lead to peptic ulcer and gastrointestinal bleeding.
Kidney function also may be compromised with NSAID use. COX inhibition causes sodium and
water retention and may lead to acute kidney damage. NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients
with chronic kidney disease.
Possibly because of their effect on kidney function, NSAIDs also may lead to an increase in
blood pressure.
COX enzymes are found in the vascular epithelium and platelet cells. The physiologic
imbalance caused by COX inhibition with NSAIDs may lead to a slight increase in
cardiovascular events, such as stroke and myocardial infarction.
Techniques/Procedures
No optimal dosing of NSAIDs exists with regard to the management of hip osteoarthritis.
NSAIDs have varying half-life and potency values; therefore, their dosing and frequency are
different.
Nonselective COX inhibitors are associated with substantial gastrointestinal adverse effects.
Prescribing a gastroprotective agent, such a proton pump inhibitor, may decrease the rate of
upper gastrointestinal bleeds, accounting for most gastrointestinal events associated with
NSAIDs; however, it will not decrease the risk of serious lower gastrointestinal events.
Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) are associated with the safest gastrointestinal adverse
effect profile of all available NSAIDs; however, similar COX-2 inhibitors (rofecoxib) have been
pulled from the market because of concerns for increased serious cardiovascular events.
Outcomes
Several randomized controlled trials have demonstrated improved hip osteoarthritis pain and
function with NSAIDs; however, these trials had a restricted timeline to a maximum of 3
months.
Celecoxib has been shown to be as effective as naproxen in the management of hip
osteoarthritis pain.5
NSAIDs are commonly prescribed for acute and chronic pain conditions because they are
powerful medications. Gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and renal adverse effects restrict their

long-term use. These drugs should be prescribed at the lowest dose and for the shortest
duration possible. NSAIDs are very reasonable medications to use during acute arthritic flares.

Outcomes
NSAIDs are some of the most prescribed medications for the management of arthritis.
Although NSAIDs effectively control pain, the associated adverse effect profile decreases
their long-term utility. The most common adverse effect is gastrointestinal ulcers in the
upper and lower gastrointestinal tract. Although COX-2 selective inhibitors are
associated with lower rates of gastrointestinal adverse effects, they may result in renal
and cardiovascular complications, and their use is contraindicated in some patients with
cardiac and renal comorbidities.
Intra-articular Corticosteroids
Intra-articular corticosteroid injections decrease local inflammation and have a substantial
positive effect with regard to pain control in patients with hip osteoarthritis, at least in the
short-term. Several randomized controlled trials have demonstrated this effect compared with
a placebo.6-8
No long-term data are available on the efficacy of repeated injections, and the safety and
efficacy of long-term therapy is unknown.
Contraindications
Patients may have local or systemic contraindications to a corticosteroid injection. Some
patients have strong sensitivities to commercial corticosteroids, resulting in flushing,
tachycardia, or anxiety. Occasionally, transient but severe hyperglycemia will occur in patients
with poorly controlled diabetes. Local soft-tissue contraindications include concern for
infection or fracture.
Corticosteroid use may lead to skin depigmentation and tendon and ligament atrophy. Precise
placement of the medication is paramount.
Particular attention should be given to the timing of intra-articular injection and future THA
because short time frames have been associated with an increased rate of septic arthritis.9 In
general, THA should be delayed.

Techniques/Procedures
Although hip injection with the use of anatomic landmarks is possible,10 the large soft-tissue
envelope makes accurate needle placement in the hip joint more difficult than in the knee.
Several ultrasonographic- and fluoroscopic- guided techniques exist.11,12 Needle insertion
usually is anterolateral or lateral, just proximal or in line with the greater trochanter.
Several corticosteroid formulations exist, such as methylprednisolone, triamcinolone, and
betamethasone. These can be injected with or without a local anesthetic.
Outcomes
Although clinically beneficial in the short-term, the long-term efficacy and safety of
corticosteroid injections is unknown. The safety, frequency, and cost-effectiveness of repeated
injections for the management of hip osteoarthritis have not been established (Resource 3).
Physical Therapy
The AAOS Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Osteoarthritis of
the Hip reports a high level of evidence in favor of physical therapy in the management of hip
osteoarthritis. Several high-quality studies have shown the advantages of various protocols.
Although the spectrum of exercises is diverse, a targeted, consistent, and supervised
strengthening, stretching, and functional motion routine may be useful in improving function
in patients with hip osteoarthritis.13,14 However, the available evidence is split, with some
high-quality trials showing no improvement in functional outcomes15 or pain13,14 in patients
who undergo physical therapy versus a placebo. Physical therapy is a very low-risk treatment
option, with only direct and indirect costs of participation and time to definitive management
as potential disadvantages.
The mechanism via which physical therapy may improve hip osteoarthritis function likely is
multifaceted. Aspects of neuronal pain modulation, improvement in functional strength, and
improvements in functional range of motion that compensate for painful arthritis may be
involved.
Contraindications

7/12

No absolute contraindication to physical therapy exists; however, patients with marked
osteoarthritis likely will not benefit from treatment via physical therapy. The initiation of
physical therapy may be very painful for and limit participation by some patients. The degree
of hip arthritis may make physical therapy attempts futile. The financial burden of a trial of
physical therapy also must be considered.
Most physical therapy trials involve patients with mild to moderate osteoarthritis.
Techniques/Procedures
The range of physical therapy programs and techniques is diverse. The general similarities are
consistency and a focus on functional strengthening. Some evidence supports adjunct
modalities, such as manipulation, massage, and ultrasonography.16,17
Other Common Treatment Options
Nonsteroidal Intra-articular Injections
The AAOS Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Osteoarthritis of
the Hip recommends against the use of hyaluronic acid for the management of hip
osteoarthritis.18 Hyaluronic acid has not been shown to be more effective than a placebo in
the management of hip pain or function.
No high-quality studies are available on the injection of other products, such as platelet-rich
plasma or bone marrow aspirate.
Nutraceuticals
Glucosamine does not improve pain and function in patients with hip osteoarthritis compared
with a placebo.19
No evidence shows that chondroitin improves hip osteoarthritis.
Aside from cost, the risk associated with these supplements is low; however, the sourcing of
some supplements may be suspect because they are not subject to the same regulatory
standards as medications.
Bracing
The hip joint is particularly challenging to brace. No good functional bracing solution exists.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:51 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001024
8/12

Canes or other walking aids may help decrease joint reaction forces in the hip.
Weight Loss
The AAOS Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Osteoarthritis of
the Hip does not comment on weight loss as a strategy for nonsurgical pain control; however,
it states that moderate evidence suggests that obesity may lead to lower absolute outcomes
after THA. Limited evidence shows that patients with obesity who undergo THA experience
higher rates of postoperative dislocations, superficial wound infections, and blood loss.
Weight loss is associated with a beneficial, dose-dependent effect on knee pain in patients with
knee osteoarthritis.20 The same benefit from decreased joint reactive forces is expected in the
hips; however, this has not been proven.
